title: Why Enterprise AI Needs a Semantic Layer
text:
For years, enterprise data strategies have focused on making data more accessible. Organizations consolidated information into data warehouses and lakehouses, built data pipelines and APIs, and introduced self-service analytics so that more people could use data in decision-making.
Generative AI takes accessibility another step forward. Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) allows language models to retrieve relevant information from enterprise sources, while AI agents can increasingly query databases, call APIs, and interact directly with business systems.
But access to data is not the same as understanding it. Consider a simple question at a bank: “What is the total relationship value of this customer?”
Answering it requires more than retrieving the customer’s records. The system needs to understand what constitutes a customer, whether accounts should be aggregated at an individual or household level, which products are included in relationship value, how balances should be calculated, which source is authoritative, and whether the person or agent making the request is permitted to access the underlying information.
Humans often resolve these questions using institutional knowledge. An experienced analyst knows which definitions to use, which systems to trust, and which business rules apply. An AI system cannot be expected to infer those meanings reliably from raw data alone.
This is the emerging challenge for enterprise AI: making business meaning as accessible to machines as the underlying data itself.

title: Why Enterprise AI Needs a Semantic Layer
text:

title: Why Enterprise AI Needs a Semantic Layer
text:
2 What Is a Semantic Layer?
A semantic layer sits between enterprise data and the people and systems that use it. Its purpose is to translate technical data structures into consistent, machine-readable business meaning.
Traditionally, semantic layers have been associated with business intelligence. They provided common definitions for measures such as revenue, customer count, deposits, or profitability so that different reports did not calculate the same metric differently.
For AI, however, the concept needs to be broader. A semantic layer can organize enterprise data around business concepts and make their meaning explicit. Depending on the architecture, it can incorporate business definitions, metrics, relationships, rules, and governed access to data.



The semantic layer provides consistent business meaning between governed enterprise data and consuming applications.


Consider a bank’s underlying data. These fields tell a system what data exists, but not necessarily what that data means in a business context:
CUSTOMER_ID = 58291
PRODUCT_CD  = DDA
BALANCE     = 250,000
BRANCH_CD   = 104
A semantic layer can make that meaning explicit:
CUSTOMER_ID → Customer
DDA         → Demand Deposit Account
BALANCE     → Current Deposit Balance (governed business rule)

Customer → owns → Account
Account  → serviced by → Branch
Customer → belongs to → Household
The first representation exposes data. The second gives that data business meaning.

title: Why Enterprise AI Needs a Semantic Layer
text:
3 Why AI Raises the Stakes
The importance of semantic consistency increases as AI moves from answering questions to making decisions and taking actions. Consider an agent asked to identify customers eligible for a particular offer. The underlying data may be accurate, but the result can still be wrong if the agent uses the wrong definition of customer, evaluates eligibility at the individual rather than household level, includes the wrong products, or applies the wrong business rules. The issue is not simply whether AI has access to the right data. It is whether the system interprets that data within the right business context.
This becomes more consequential as AI moves closer to action:
Traditional Analytics 

Data → Analyst → Interpretation → Decision


Agentic AI

Data → AI Interpretation → Decision → Tool → Action
Semantic consistency therefore becomes more than a data-management concern. It becomes part of the control environment for enterprise AI. Business meaning, however, extends beyond definitions and rules. Enterprise knowledge is also deeply relational.

title: Why Enterprise AI Needs a Semantic Layer
text:
4 Knowledge Graphs: Making Relationships Explicit
A customer owns accounts, belongs to a household, may own a business, has loans secured by collateral, and interacts with employees. A knowledge graph makes relationships such as these explicit by representing business concepts as entities and the connections among them as relationships.
An ontology can provide the conceptual model behind this structure by defining business entities, their classifications, and the relationships among them. For example, an ontology might define checking and savings accounts as types of deposit accounts, and specify that customers can own accounts while loans can be secured by properties. The knowledge graph then represents actual customers, accounts, loans, and properties using those concepts and relationships.



A simplified knowledge graph representing relationships among banking entities.


Knowledge graphs can complement the semantic layer by making relationships among business concepts explicit and machine-readable. A useful distinction is that a semantic layer helps define what business concepts mean and how they should be interpreted, an ontology defines how those concepts are structured and related, and a knowledge graph represents the actual entities and connections among them.
For example, a semantic layer might define what customer, deposit balance, or household means and which rules govern their use. A knowledge graph can represent which accounts a customer owns, which household the customer belongs to, which businesses the customer is connected to, and how customers, loans, and properties are related.
This becomes important when AI needs to answer questions that depend on relationships, paths, and connected information, rather than simply finding a relevant document.

title: Why Enterprise AI Needs a Semantic Layer
text:
5 GraphRAG: Retrieving Connected Context
Traditional RAG typically retrieves information based on semantic similarity. This works well when the answer can be found in relevant passages, but enterprise questions are not always similarity problems.
Consider:

Which commercial customers have loans secured by properties affected by this policy change, and who manages those relationships?

The answer may not exist in any single document or database record. It may require connecting a policy to applicable loan types, loans to collateral, collateral to customers, and customers to relationship managers.
This is where GraphRAG becomes useful. GraphRAG combines retrieval-augmented generation with graph-structured knowledge, allowing retrieval to incorporate entities and relationships rather than relying only on semantically similar content.



Traditional RAG retrieves semantically relevant content, while GraphRAG uses entities and relationships to retrieve connected context.


The approaches are complementary rather than competing. An enterprise architecture may use both vector and graph retrieval to construct context for the model. The objective is not simply to retrieve information that resembles the question. It is to construct the right context for the task.

title: Why Enterprise AI Needs a Semantic Layer
section: 6 Context Engineering: Building the Right Context for AI
text:
6 Context Engineering: Building the Right Context for AI
RAG and GraphRAG address an important question: How do we retrieve information relevant to a task? But retrieval is only one part of what an AI system needs.
An enterprise agent may require business definitions from a semantic layer, connected knowledge from a knowledge graph, structured data from operational systems, relevant documents, memory, policies, tools, permissions, and the current state of a workflow.
The challenge is therefore broader than retrieval. Context engineering determines what information and capabilities an AI system needs for a particular task and assembles them into usable context.
More context is not necessarily better. Excessive or irrelevant information can increase cost and latency, obscure relevant information, and introduce conflicts. The objective is to provide the right context for the task.
Each component contributes something different:

Semantic layer — What does this information mean?
RAG — What information is relevant?
Knowledge graph — How are these things connected?
Memory — What should the system remember?
Tools — What can the agent do?
Permissions and policies — What is the agent allowed to do?

Context engineering goes beyond retrieving information. It is the discipline of assembling the information, meaning, capabilities, and constraints an AI system needs for a particular task.
As AI moves from answering questions to performing work, engineering the right context becomes part of building the AI system itself.

title: Why Enterprise AI Needs a Semantic Layer
section: 7 The Emerging Enterprise AI Context Architecture
text:
7 The Emerging Enterprise AI Context Architecture
Context engineering addresses what an AI system needs for a particular task. At enterprise scale, a broader question emerges: How should organizations provide that context consistently, securely, and with appropriate governance? At enterprise scale, AI needs a governed path from data to meaning to context.



A governed enterprise AI architecture connecting data, business meaning, task-specific context, and AI outcomes.


That path does not require every AI application to use every component. A policy assistant may work well with conventional RAG. An analytics assistant may rely primarily on governed metrics and structured data. A use case involving complex relationships may benefit from a knowledge graph and GraphRAG. The architecture should be shaped by the task.
What matters is that the path from enterprise data to AI context remains governed. Business definitions need ownership. Sources need authority and lineage. Context needs appropriate access controls. Retrieval needs evaluation. And the information supplied to an AI system needs to remain consistent with the permissions and policies governing the underlying data.
As AI systems become more autonomous, the quality of their decisions and actions will depend not only on the intelligence of the model, but also on the quality of the context architecture surrounding it.
The semantic layer therefore becomes part of a broader foundation for enabling AI systems to interpret enterprise data within the context in which it is used.

title: Why Enterprise AI Needs a Semantic Layer
section: 8 Conclusion: Business Meaning as AI Infrastructure
text:
8 Conclusion: Business Meaning as AI Infrastructure
Enterprise AI is making organizational knowledge increasingly accessible. But access alone does not create understanding.
As AI moves from answering questions to making decisions and taking actions, organizations need machine-readable definitions, relationships, rules, and context. The semantic layer therefore becomes more than an analytics abstraction—it becomes part of the foundation for how enterprise AI interprets and uses business information.
The enterprise AI challenge is no longer simply making data accessible. It is making business meaning machine-readable.

title: Fix the Data Before You Pick the Model
text:
I built and tested an AI assistant using five public banking regulatory documents to understand what improves answer quality. Across 26 test questions, improving document preparation and retrieval increased answer completeness from 42% to 95% on the 19 questions scored for completeness. Switching language models made a much smaller difference: just one question.
The models differed more noticeably in how they handled information they couldn’t find.

title: Fix the Data Before You Pick the Model
text:
1 Why I built it
Many enterprise AI use cases involve answering questions from internal documents, policies, and procedures. Banks are increasingly evaluating these systems, often through vendor demonstrations that showcase what the technology can do.
But a successful demonstration tells us little about where a system fails, why it fails, or how reliably it answers questions. I wanted to understand what actually improves answer quality: better models, better documents, or better retrieval.

title: Fix the Data Before You Pick the Model
text:
2 What I built
The assistant answers questions using five publicly available regulatory documents, citing the source document and page so readers can verify its responses. When the documents do not contain enough information to answer a question, the assistant is instructed to say so.







Document
Issuer




SR 26-2, Supervisory Guidance on Model Risk Management (2026)
Federal Reserve, FDIC, OCC


SR 11-7, Supervisory Guidance on Model Risk Management (2011, superseded)
Federal Reserve, OCC


AI Risk Management Framework 1.0 (AI 100-1)
NIST


Generative AI Profile (AI 600-1)
NIST


Interagency Guidance on Third-Party Relationships: Risk Management (2023)
Federal Reserve, FDIC, OCC



Each question runs through the same steps:

Retrieve: Search documents using both semantic similarity and exact terms, then combine the results.
Provide context: Pass the five most relevant passages, along with neighboring passages, to the language model.
Generate an answer: Instruct the model to answer using only the retrieved material, cite its sources, or decline when the information is insufficient.

I developed and tested the assistant locally using Llama 3.1 8B. The publicly available version uses Claude Haiku 5.5 and is hosted online. The code and evaluation framework are available on GitHub.
View the code on GitHub
Try the live regulatory guidance assistant

title: Fix the Data Before You Pick the Model
text:
3 How I tested it
I developed 26 test questions covering the five regulatory documents. Twenty-one were answerable from the documents, including definitions, lists, specific terminology, and comparisons across sources. Five were intentionally outside the documents’ scope, covering topics such as Basel III capital requirements, the EU AI Act, and CCAR stress testing.
The unanswerable questions were equally important. A reliable assistant needs to recognize when the available evidence is insufficient rather than generate a plausible but unsupported response.
For 19 answerable questions, I created an answer key specifying the facts required for a complete response. A script checked whether those facts appeared in each answer using text matching, rather than relying on another AI model to judge correctness. Two open-ended questions were excluded from automated completeness scoring because valid responses could take different approaches that a fixed answer key would not reliably capture.
I applied the same final answer key to the saved responses from all nine experimental runs, ensuring consistent comparisons. Every run tested all 26 questions, including those designed to trigger appropriate refusals.
To check the automated scoring, all 19 scored answers from run 9 were reviewed against the answer key with AI assistance. The AI-assisted review agreed with the automated score on 18 of 19 questions. The remaining disagreement involved an overly strict answer-key requirement: the response used “safely and soundly” where the key required “safe and sound.” I corrected that entry and applied the revised key consistently across all nine runs. The subsequent repeated outputs were not independently reviewed, and no answers were reviewed by an independent human expert.

title: Fix the Data Before You Pick the Model
text:
4 What moved the numbers
Across nine experimental runs, answer completeness increased from 42% to 95% on the 19 scored questions. Most of the improvement came from preparing the documents and refining retrieval, rather than changing the language model. All five out-of-scope questions were correctly refused in every run.

Every run was scored against the same final answer key. After correcting two entries to recognize equivalent wording, I rescored all nine runs to ensure consistent comparisons.
With 19 scored questions, each question represents approximately five percentage points, so runs 7 through 9 differ by at most one question. Moving search into the hosted application changed one of the five retrieved passages for one question, despite using the same embedding model. The difference may have resulted from how embeddings were generated in the hosted environment, but this was not independently verified. The decline in run 8 was attributable to a single answer in which Llama omitted the condition that early use requires circumstances such as an urgent business need. Given the same passages in run 9, Claude retained that qualification. The publicly available assistant uses the configuration from run 9.
Three runs changed more than one setting. Run 5 added neighboring passages and enlarged the model’s context window to 8,192 tokens so longer inputs would not be truncated. Run 7 removed commentary pages and corrected special characters that interfered with keyword search. Run 9 changed the model and its sampling settings: Llama ran at temperature 0, while Claude used its default settings. All three Claude executions scored 95%. The answer-generation instructions remained identical across all nine runs.
The largest improvement came from labeling each passage with its source document, increasing completeness from 42% to 63%. Removing irrelevant content also mattered. The Federal Register version of the third-party guidance includes 24 pages of background and responses to public comments. Some of these pages use headings similar to the actual guidance, causing the assistant to retrieve commentary instead of authoritative content.
The retrieval logs show an important distinction. By run 3, search placed the correct document among the top five retrieved passages for all 21 answerable questions, up from 17 in run 1 and 19 in run 2. Yet answer completeness continued improving from 74% to 95%. Subsequent changes addressed passage selection, context availability, and document quality. Retrieving the correct document was no longer the primary obstacle; finding and using the right evidence within it remained a challenge.
Semantic search can recognize relationships between terms, but it does not guarantee that the most relevant passages will be retrieved. In this experiment, a question used “worsened” while NIST’s guidance used “exacerbated.” The relevant passage was not among those retrieved, so the language model never received the information needed to answer completely. Adding the regulatory term through a curated glossary helped keyword search retrieve the correct passage, improving answer completeness from 84% to 89%—one additional complete answer. This illustrates how a business-governed vocabulary can improve retrieval without changing the underlying language model.

title: Fix the Data Before You Pick the Model
text:
5 Grounded Is Not Correct
A common approach to evaluating retrieval-based AI systems is to ask a language model whether an answer is supported by its sources. In one experimental run, the model-based evaluator rated all 20 assessed answers as fully grounded. Yet the separate answer-key evaluation identified five incomplete or unanswered responses among the 19 questions scored for completeness.
These evaluations measured different things. Groundedness asks whether an answer is supported by the retrieved material. It does not necessarily establish whether the answer is complete, factually accurate, or attributed to the correct document.
Two failures illustrate the distinction:

An invented list. Asked to identify the stages of the third-party relationship lifecycle, the assistant included “Onboarding” and “Offboarding.” Neither appears in the guidance, which identifies planning, due diligence and selection, contract negotiation, ongoing monitoring, and termination. The evaluator nevertheless rated the response fully grounded.
A misattributed quotation. Asked how expectations for effective challenge changed between SR 11-7 and SR 26-2, the assistant quoted language from SR 26-2 but attributed it to SR 11-7. The quotation was real, but its attribution was incorrect.

In this experiment, the same language model generated and evaluated the answers. That creates an important limitation: a model’s assessment of its own output is not a substitute for independent evaluation. Subject-matter experts, explicit answer criteria, and separate checks for completeness and citation accuracy provide stronger evidence of reliability.

title: Fix the Data Before You Pick the Model
text:
6 What the Model Changed
With the same hosted retrieval configuration, Llama 3.1 8B achieved 89% completeness, compared with 95% for Claude Haiku 5.5. The difference was just one question out of 19, too small to establish a meaningful performance advantage. Llama had also reached 95% in an earlier run using the original search configuration.
Both models missed the fifth category of NIST’s GOVERN function. The failure could reflect missing retrieval evidence or the models’ inability to use information they received. Either way, changing models alone did not resolve it.
The more noticeable difference was how the models handled missing information:

Llama filled gaps. In earlier runs, it sometimes generated plausible content when the retrieved passages were insufficient, including invented third-party lifecycle stages. Some claims also lacked citations.
Claude acknowledged gaps. It explicitly identified when the retrieved passages lacked sufficient detail, cited its claims, and flagged that the SR 11-7 source was labeled superseded.

Better retrieval gets the right evidence to the model. Model selection still matters, particularly when the available evidence is incomplete.

title: Fix the Data Before You Pick the Model
text:
7 What This Means for Banks
Selecting a capable model is only one part of building a reliable system. The quality of the information available to the model, how that information is retrieved, and how answers are evaluated can be equally important.

Invest in knowledge readiness. Identify authoritative sources, remove outdated or irrelevant material, preserve document context, and make ownership and versioning explicit. These are not simply document-management activities; they directly influence AI performance.
Evaluate the entire system. A successful demonstration or high groundedness score is not sufficient evidence of reliability. Banks should separately test retrieval accuracy, answer completeness, citation attribution, and the ability to refuse questions when evidence is insufficient.
Reuse what works. Document preparation, retrieval services, access controls, and evaluation frameworks should become shared enterprise capabilities. This reduces duplication and makes it easier to apply consistent controls across AI use cases.

Reliable enterprise AI requires trusted knowledge, effective retrieval, and evidence that the system works as intended.

title: Fix the Data Before You Pick the Model
text:
8 Before Putting It Into Production
The experiment used five public documents and a relatively small test set. A production system handling internal policies, procedures, or regulatory guidance would require more rigorous validation.
Before deployment, I would prioritize nine controls:

Build an expert-reviewed answer key. Include expected facts, acceptable variations, and questions the system should refuse. Reserve a separate set of previously unseen questions for independent validation.
Evaluate retrieval separately. Confirm that the correct source passages are retrieved before assessing the generated answer.
Verify citation accuracy. Check that each claim is supported by the cited document and page, not merely by another retrieved passage.
Curate authoritative documents. Remove irrelevant commentary, identify superseded guidance, and maintain clear document ownership and versioning.
Maintain a reviewed terminology glossary. Map common business language to regulatory terminology without introducing unintended interpretations.
Test document extraction. Verify that tables, images, footnotes, and multi-page lists survive ingestion accurately.
Test appropriate refusals. Include questions outside the approved knowledge base and cases where retrieved evidence is incomplete.
Run regression tests after every change. Reevaluate the full question set when documents, retrieval logic, prompts, or models change.
Retest model upgrades. Treat a model change as a system change requiring validation, even when the underlying documents remain the same.

These controls do not guarantee that an AI assistant will always produce correct answers. They provide a more defensible basis for determining whether the system is reliable enough for its intended use.

title: Fix the Data Before You Pick the Model
text:
9 Limitations
This was a small experiment involving five public regulatory documents and 26 test questions. Nineteen questions were scored for answer completeness using a predefined answer key, while five tested appropriate refusals. Two open-ended questions were excluded from automated completeness scoring.

No held-out evaluation. System improvements were made after reviewing failures on the same 26 questions, including glossary mappings and the exclusion of irrelevant commentary pages. Two answer-key entries were also corrected during evaluation. The 95% completeness result may therefore overestimate performance on unseen questions. A separate set of new questions, developed independently and never used for tuning, would help determine whether the improvements generalize.
Small test set. With 19 scored questions, a single answer changes the completeness score by approximately five percentage points.
Limited document complexity. The experiment used a small collection of public regulatory documents rather than a large enterprise knowledge base containing conflicting policies, access restrictions, and frequent updates.
Question design. Many questions explicitly identified the relevant document, making retrieval easier than it would be for less specific employee questions.
Automated scoring. The answer key measured whether required facts appeared in responses. It did not systematically detect every unsupported addition, misleading statement, or citation error. Expected source pages were recorded for only eight of the 21 answerable questions, limiting the ability to measure passage-level retrieval performance.
Limited model comparison. The results reflect specific models, prompts, documents, and retrieval configurations. They do not establish that one model will consistently outperform another.

The results show how specific engineering changes affected this assistant. They do not establish how well the approach would perform across larger document collections or different use cases. I would need a larger question set, independent reviewers, and actual enterprise documents before drawing broader conclusions.
